cards.explanation: The answer is False. Solomon, king of Israel, says "Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife." (Proverbs 17:1) The feast loses because of the strife that comes with it. A dry bite in peace beats a big spread with a fight going on, friends.
The answer is the wise servant, friends. The text says "A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son…" Think about that. A servant over a son. I'd have to read that twice.

The answer is a share of the inheritance, bakers. The wise servant will "…share his inheritance as one of the brothers." A servant sitting at the family table as one of the brothers. I'd be grinning over my plate too.

The answer is hearts, friends. "A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts." Fire tests metal, and the LORD tests the heart. Heat in my oven can only show me what's on the outside of a cookie.

The answer is mocks, bakers. The saying is "He who mocks the poor insults their Maker…" Making fun of the poor lands on the One who made them. That's a heavy thing to say, and it's right there in the text.

The answer is True, friends. The second half of the verse says "whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished." Gloating over somebody's disaster is not a free move. The text says it comes with a price.
The answer is lying lips, bakers. "Eloquent words are unfit for a fool; how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!" Lying lips on a ruler are the worse thing. That's the comparison the saying makes.
The answer is concealing the offense, friends. "Whoever conceals an offense promotes love…" Covering it up instead of announcing it grows love. Keeping a lid on it saves a lot of friendships.

The answer is the man of discernment, bakers. "A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool." A rebuke on one side and a hundred lashes on the other. And it's the rebuke that cuts deeper into the man of discernment. I think that's because he actually listens, and the words land.

The answer is False, friends. The verse says "It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly." The bear is the better meeting, and the fool in his folly is worse. And I wouldn't want either one in my bakery.

The answer is False, bakers. The verse says "If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house." The word is never, with no "in time" attached. Paying back good with evil is a serious thing.
The answer is releasing a flood, friends. "To start a quarrel is to release a flood…" Once the gate is open, you can't call the water back. The first cross word is the easy part.
The answer is before it breaks out, bakers. The verse says "…abandon the dispute before it breaks out." Walk away while it's still small. A flood is a lot easier to stop when it's only a drip.

The answer is both of them, friends. "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD." He names both verdicts. The word is both, and avoiding just one isn't what the verse says. A judge can't pick a favorite way to get it wrong.

The answer is wisdom, bakers. The question is why the fool should have money in his hand "…with no intention of buying wisdom?" The money is there, but the plan to buy wisdom isn't. That's the sad part of the saying.
The answer is all, friends. "A friend loves at all times…" Not just the easy times, not just the party. All of them, the good ones and the rough ones.
The answer is True, bakers. The verse says "…a brother is born for adversity." The same verse says "A friend loves at all times…" Hard times are where those two show up.

The answer is a man lacking judgment, friends. The text calls him "A man lacking judgment…" for striking hands in pledge and putting up security for his neighbor. That's the exact label the proverb gives him. It's a plain warning about promising to cover someone else.

The answer is True, bakers. The text says "The one with a perverse heart finds no good…" The verse goes right on to the deceitful tongue falling into trouble. A twisted heart doesn't land on anything good.

The answer is that it dries up the bones, friends. "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones." Joy is medicine, and a broken spirit does the opposite. It's a picture of how much the inside affects the outside.
The answer is to twist justice, bakers. The wicked man takes the bribe "…to subvert the course of justice." That's what the covert bribe is for. The aim is to turn justice off its course.

The answer is to the ends of the earth, friends. "…the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth." Right beside it, "Wisdom is the focus of the discerning…" Two pictures side by side: eyes locked on one thing, and eyes all over the map.

The answer is bitterness, bakers. "A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him." Both parents feel it, one with grief and one with bitterness. It's a hard line, and the text just says it plainly.

The answer is innocent, friends. "It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty." Punishing someone who did nothing wrong is not good. The verse says it plainly. The same saying says it about flogging a noble for his honesty too.
The answer is restrains, bakers. "A man of knowledge restrains his words…" He holds back what he says. And a calm spirit goes right along with it.

The answer is when he keeps silent, friends. "Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue." Keep quiet and you get credit for wisdom you may not have. I could use that on a few Tuesdays.
